newsitem.title: BRAZIL: SOYBEANS - Rains delay early Brazil harvest.
newsitem.headline: SOYBEANS - Rains delay early Brazil harvest.

text.p: Excess rains were delaying the harvest of early-cycle soybeans in the Brazilian state of Mato Grosso, raising fears of a delay in February shipments which could clog up ports for several months.
Heavy rains have hit the north of Mato Grosso for the last two weeks, suspending the harvest of so-called precocious cycle soybeans and causing a drop in quality.

"The harvest has stopped because of the rain," said Tony Fagundes at the Cooperlucas cooperative. "It's a very big concern but the forecasters tell us the weather should start clearing up from tomorrow so we're hopeful."
Luiz Duarte, policy adviser at the Mato Grosso agricultural secretariat, said the state was forecast to produce 5.39 million tonnes in 1996/97.

Of this, 500,000 tonnes would be from the precocious cycle crop, said Fagundes, adding that 85 to 90 percent of the crop had already been committed to insure growers against a price drop once regions like Parana start harvesting.
Traders said a lot of soybeans had been sold for Feb 15-March 15 shipment to take advantage of higher nearby premiums, and any delay in early shipments would cause problems for months.

"We are concerned," said a trader. "There is a very large schedule for early beans. In the case of Paranagua (port) it's a bit of a disaster because if those early shipments are delayed, it takes months and months to recover."

"There's not much in stock to cover for any delay," said another trader. "There is also a problem with quality. Too much cloud cover could affect the production of the regular cycle beans which need a certain amount of sunlight."
Once the rain stopped in Mato Grosso, all the growers would rush to ship their product at once, traders predicted.
"Paranagua is already a port that doesn't work too well. What will already be an awkward situation will simply be a bit worse this year," a trader said.
"If we can't get the product out of Brazil in the short-term, people will start buying from the U.S. instead," he said, adding that tight U.S. supply was keeping the market nervous.

Although worries about the situation in Mato Grosso were supporting the market, this was counterbalanced by rains this week in the key producing region of Rio Grande do Sul which doused concerns that drought would cause crop losses there.
"We've got fantastic rains, better than anyone was expecting," said a trader based in Rio Grande do Sul.

Most cooperatives in the south said the soybean crop was unscathed by a recent dry spell and corn had suffered the most. But some reported a drop in soybean production ranging from five to 20 percent.
Export trade slowed slightly from the previous week, with Europe remaining the main destination.
Dealers also reported talk that China was selling U.S. soymeal stocked in its ports for immediate shipment and buying South American soymeal for shipment further out.
"There's been around one million tonnes traded, between meal and beans, in the last two weeks. That's not only for export but includes the internal market as well," said a trader.
Most trade was in soybeans with very few soymeal and soyoil sales as most crushers were still closed for maintenance work, although some were reopening as the first of the Mato Grosso crop came in.
"Crushing is going to be very low in Jan-Feb, some 60,000 tonnes," said Fagundes at Cooperlucas. "But from February 10 all the crushers will be open again."
"There's a certain amount of crushers on the markets selling their beans (because of higher nearby premiums)," said one trader. "We've seen some fairly good volume."
